## Functions

### `convolution_interpolation`

```julia
convolution_interpolation(knots, values::AbstractArray{T,N}; kwargs...) where {T,N}
```

Create a convolution-based interpolation object with automatic optimization and boundary handling.

#### Arguments

  * `knots`: Vector or range (1D) or tuple of vectors/ranges (N-D) of grid coordinates.
  * `values`: Array of values at the grid points.

#### Keyword Arguments

  * `kernel::Symbol=:auto`: Convolution kernel to use. The default depends on the dimension, to reflect the tensor-product cost: `:b7` in 1-2D, `:b5` in 3D, `:a4` in 4-5D and `:a3` above. On a grid with a nonuniform axis the default from 4D is `:n3`.

      * `a`-series: `:a0` (nearest), `:a1` (linear), `:a3` (cubic), `:a4` (quartic), `:a5` (quintic), `:a7` (septic)
      * `b`-series: `:b5`, `:b7`, `:b9`, `:b11`, `:b13`
      * `:n3` (cubic): the nonuniform implementation of `:a3`. `:a3` and `:n3` are interchangeable — a uniform grid always evaluates with the fast `:a3` kernel, a nonuniform grid with the `:n3` weights, whichever name is given.

    `:a0`, `:a1`, and all `b`-series kernels work on both uniform and nonuniform grids. `:a3` falls back to `:n3` on nonuniform grids (same order, nonuniform weights). `:a4`, `:a5` and `:a7` are uniform-only and raise an error on nonuniform grids.
  * `fast::Bool=true`: Store the integral tails of antiderivatives at construction, so that every evaluation stays O(1). With `fast=false`, antiderivatives are summed over all coefficients at every evaluation (O(data) per evaluation, no stored tails), which avoids the tail arrays for a few integrals of a large dataset. Only affects `derivative < 0`.
  * `extrap=:throw`: Behavior outside the grid domain. Options: `:throw`, `:flat`, `:line` or `:natural` (uniform grids only).
  * `bc=nothing`: Boundary condition for the ghost values at the domain edges. `nothing` lets the grid decide: `:detect` on a uniform grid (see below), and on a nonuniform grid `:kernel`, the kernel's own extrapolation, which is the only rule there. On uniform grids the options are `:detect`, `:poly`, `:linear` and `:quadratic`; giving one on a nonuniform grid is an error.
  * `derivative::Union{Int,NTuple{N,Int}}=0`: Derivative order to evaluate, one value for all dimensions or one per dimension, up to each kernel's limit on the grid of that axis (the kernel tables in the README): on a uniform grid 1 for the `a` kernels, 3 for `:b5` and 5 for `:b7`-`:b13`; on a nonuniform grid 3, 5, 7, 9 and 11 for `:b5`-`:b13`. The limits follow from the convergence: on a uniform grid the `b` kernels reproduce polynomials through degree 6, so derivative `k` converges at order `7 - k`, and orders above 5 are excluded as sub-second-order; on a nonuniform grid they reproduce their full degree `p`, derivative `k` converges at order `p + 1 - k`, and the limit is the last continuous derivative, `p - 2`. Rounding in the data is amplified by `h^-k` on every grid, so high orders on fine grids need `BigFloat` data. `derivative=-m` evaluates the m-fold antiderivative, anchored at zero (with its first `m - 1` derivatives) at the leftmost interior knot of each integrated axis, on uniform grids only, up to order 2 for `:a0`/`:a1`, 4 for the other `a`-series kernels, 6 for `:b5` and 8 for `:b7`-`:b13`. Orders may be mixed per dimension, e.g. `(-2, 0)` or `(-1, 1)`, with or without stored tails (see `fast`).
  * `lazy::Union{Nothing,Bool}=nothing`: When `true`, skip ghost point expansion at construction time. Ghost values are computed on the fly only when evaluating near boundaries, with exactly the values eager expansion would store, saving memory and construction time. When `false`, all ghost points are expanded at construction. The default, `nothing`, chooses lazy mode on uniform grids (no antiderivatives) when eager expansion would build more than 2²⁷ coefficients (1 GiB in `Float64`) or compute more than 2²⁴ ghost points (roughly a second of construction), and eager mode otherwise. Nonuniform grids compute their ghost values at construction, so `lazy=true` is an error there.

#### Returns

A `ConvolutionExtrapolation` object callable at arbitrary points within (or, depending on `extrap`, outside) the grid domain.

#### Performance

  * Construction is dominated by the ghost values on a uniform grid, which `lazy=true` defers to evaluation, and by the per-interval weight tables of the `b` kernels on a nonuniform grid.
  * Evaluation is allocation-free and independent of the grid size on a uniform axis; a nonuniform axis adds a binary search for the cell. Boundary cells are slightly slower in lazy mode. The benchmark pages on convinterp.org give timings.

#### Examples

```julia
# 1D interpolation
x = range(0, 2π, length=50)
itp = convolution_interpolation(x, sin.(x))
itp(1.0)

# 2D with lazy construction
x = range(0, 1, length=100)
y = range(0, 1, length=100)
vals = [sin(2π*xi)*cos(2π*yi) for xi in x, yi in y]
itp = convolution_interpolation((x, y), vals, lazy=true)
itp(0.3, 0.7)

# First derivative
itp_d = convolution_interpolation(x, sin.(x), derivative=1)
itp_d(1.0)  # ≈ cos(1.0)

# High-dimensional with lazy mode (recommended)
knots_5d = ntuple(_ -> range(0, 1, length=20), 5)
vals_5d = rand(20,20,20,20,20)
itp = convolution_interpolation(knots_5d, vals_5d, lazy=true)
itp(0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5)
```

See also: [`ConvolutionInterpolation`](@ref), [`ConvolutionExtrapolation`](@ref).

```julia
convolution_interpolation(points::AbstractMatrix, values::AbstractVector; kwargs...)
```

Scattered-data convolution interpolation. Each column of `points` is one data point (`D x Np`); `values` holds the corresponding data values.

Fits the data with `fit_scattered` and wraps the fitted grid in the standard interpolant, so evaluation, derivatives, and integrals work exactly as for gridded data. The default `mode = :smooth` smooths the data with the smoothing chosen automatically, which suits measured, noisy data (to see the chosen `lambda` and the estimated noise, call `fit_scattered` directly); for trusted, noise-free data use `mode = :exact`, whose interpolant passes through the data. Unlike the gridded constructors, which always interpolate, the scattered path smooths by default, because scattered data are usually measurements. All `fit_scattered` keyword arguments are accepted, including `grid`, `alpha` and `ratio` for adaptive or user-supplied knot axes, plus `derivative`, which is forwarded to the interpolant, and `extrap`. On a uniform grid the boundary condition is fixed to `:poly` for consistency with the fit; on a nonuniform grid the interpolant's own ghost extrapolation is the one the fit used. A nonuniform grid gives a nonuniform interpolant (`:b5` by default for `:smooth` in 1-3D and for `:exact` in 1D, `:n3` otherwise; see `fit_scattered`): no antiderivatives (`derivative = -1`) and no lazy ghosts.

```julia
# 500 scattered points in 2D, one per column
pts = rand(2, 500)
# the signal at the points
vals = [sin(3p[1]) * cos(2p[2]) for p in eachcol(pts)]
# measured with noise
noisy = vals .+ 0.05 .* randn(500)
# smoothing chosen automatically
itp = convolution_interpolation(pts, noisy)
# close to the noise-free value
itp(0.4, 0.6)

# noise-free data: interpolate exactly
itp_x = convolution_interpolation(pts, vals; mode = :exact)
# evaluate anywhere inside the data's box
itp_x(0.4, 0.6)

# knots follow the point density
itp_a = convolution_interpolation(pts, vals; mode = :exact, grid = :adaptive)
```




### `fit_scattered`

```julia
fit_scattered(points, values; kwargs...)
```

Fit scattered data with a convolution interpolant on a grid over the data's bounding box.

The tensor-product kernel basis lives on a grid covering the data's bounding box: uniform by default, or, with `grid = :adaptive`, with per-axis knots that follow the density of the points. Ghost coefficients are eliminated before the solve using the package's polynomial boundary condition (the Vandermonde ghost extrapolation of the nonuniform kernels on nonuniform grids), so the solution is a completed grid consistent with `bc = :poly`. Because the kernels are cardinal on the grid, the fitted interior coefficients are the interpolant's values at the interior knots: `fit_scattered` returns exactly the `(knots, values)` pair the gridded constructors consume.

Two modes:

  * `:smooth` (default) smooths: it minimizes `(1/n)·‖A c − f‖² + lambda·Σ_d ∫|∂_d^q s|²`, the mean squared misfit plus `lambda` times the roughness (in coordinates normalized to the bounding box, so `lambda` does not depend on the grid or the units of each axis). By default `lambda` is chosen by generalized cross-validation, so no smoothing parameter needs to be tuned. For measured data, which usually carry some noise; on noise-free data it approaches interpolation, less accurately than `:exact`. Needs more data points than the penalty's null space has dimensions: `q^D`, i.e. 125 in 3D with the default `q = 5`.
  * `:exact` interpolates: the fit passes through every data point to machine precision, and among the admissible grids the one minimizing a q-th order roughness seminorm is selected. For trusted, noise-free data only: noise is reproduced exactly and amplified between the points, most of all in derivatives.

#### Arguments

  * `points::AbstractMatrix`: `D x Np` matrix; each column is one data point.
  * `values::AbstractVector`: `Np` data values.

#### Keyword Arguments

  * `kernel::Union{Symbol,NTuple{D,Symbol}}=:auto`: on a uniform grid any kernel with a polynomial boundary-condition table (`:a3`, `:a4`, `:a5`, `:a7`, `:b5`...`:b13`); on a nonuniform grid (`grid = :adaptive` or user axes) `:n3` or a `:b` kernel, the kernels that support nonuniform grids. `:auto` depends on the mode and the dimension. For `:smooth`, and for `:exact` in 1D, it is `:b5` in 1-3D: the accuracy of a `:b` kernel at a cost that is small once a `:smooth` fit has coarsened to the grid its smoothing needs, and in 1D the fastest and most accurate `:exact` choice. Note this differs from the gridded default (`:b7` for 1-2D): for scattered data the boundary-condition tables cap all b-kernels at degree-7 reproduction, and `:b5`'s shallower ghost extrapolation gives it the lowest roundoff floor under `:cholesky`. For `:exact` on a uniform grid from 2D up the narrow kernels take over, `:a4` in 2-3D and `:a3` from 4D: the grid is then mostly gaps between the data points, where the roughness order sets the accuracy and the kernel order hardly matters, so the narrow kernels match the `:b` kernels at two to ten times less factorization time (and `:b5` falls behind them in 3D). For `:smooth` on a uniform grid the cheap kernels take over from 4D: `:a4` for 4-5D and `:a3` above. On nonuniform grids both modes use `:n3` from 4D (closed-form weights, a 4-wide stencil and no per-interval precompute). Interpolate the fitted grid with the fitting kernel.
  * `mode::Symbol=:smooth`: `:smooth` or `:exact` (see above).
  * `grid::Union{Symbol,Tuple}=:uniform`: the knot axes. `:uniform` is the uniform grid over the bounding box. `:adaptive` places the knots of each axis where they are needed, blended with the uniform knots by `alpha` and with the ratio of adjacent spacings capped at `ratio`. For `:exact` the need is the points: the knots sit at the quantiles of the coordinates along each axis, so a dense band of points gets a dense band of knots, which is what lets `:exact` interpolate clustered points at all. For `:smooth` the need is the signal: the uniform fit is made first, and its curvature along each axis places the knots — dense in a boundary layer, a step or a fast oscillation, sparse where the fit is flat — and the fit is repeated on them, with half the uniform fit's knot count unless `gridsize` says otherwise. The grid is still a tensor product, so it helps when the need is roughly separable along the axes, not for isolated features; in two or more dimensions points can still share a cell of an `:exact` grid where the clusters of several axes overlap, and `oversample` is the remedy. A tuple of strictly increasing knot vectors, one per axis, is used as given; the vectors must cover the data. Nonuniform grids give a nonuniform interpolant: no antiderivatives (`derivative = -1`) and no lazy construction. With the `:b` kernels construction costs one exact-arithmetic projection per interval, so keep their knot counts modest; `:n3` has no such cost.
  * `alpha::Real=1.0`, `ratio::Real=2.0` (`grid = :adaptive` only): the blend between uniform (`0`) and quantile (`1`) knots, and the largest allowed ratio of adjacent knot spacings. The cap keeps the nonuniform kernels and their ghost extrapolation well conditioned; raise it for strongly graded data.
  * `gridsize::Union{Symbol,Int,NTuple{D,Int}}=:auto`: interior knots per dimension. An `Int` or tuple is used as given in both modes. With `:auto`, both modes size the grid from `oversample` and the data count. `:smooth` fits on that grid first — a coarser grid could absorb part of the signal into the residual, where nothing in the fit reveals it — and then, when the fitted smoothing needs far fewer knots, refits on the grid that resolves its cutoff (about eight knots per cycle), warm-started from `lambda`. The returned grid is therefore as coarse as the fit allows; a grid much finer than the fit is ill-conditioned and would hold the smoothing short of its optimum. With user axes the knot counts are those of the axes, and `gridsize` must be `:auto`.
  * `oversample::Real=0.0`: grid knots per data spacing when `gridsize=:auto`. `0.0` selects the mode default: 0.8 for `:smooth`; for `:exact` 1.6 in 1D, 2.5 in 2D and 2.0 in 3D and above, since random points in two or more dimensions share a grid cell often enough at the 1D density that the fit goes least-squares. Points closer together than the local knot spacing cannot be interpolated separately on any grid; if `:exact` warns, raise `oversample`. `:smooth` warns when the fitted smoothing would need a finer grid than this allows (about eight knots per cycle of its cutoff): the fit may then be under-resolved, and a larger `oversample` helps.
  * `q::Union{Int,Symbol}=:auto`: order of the roughness seminorm. `:smooth` penalises the q-th differences along each axis; `:exact` the full isotropic `H^q` seminorm from 2D up, every mixed difference of total order `q` included (in 1D the two coincide). The isotropic seminorm is the one the polyharmonic splines minimise, and it decides what the completion does in the gaps between the data points, where from 2D up most of the grid lies: the axis-wise differences leave the mixed modes to the data alone, which costs accuracy from 3D up, most of all away from the data's centre. It favours features without a preferred direction; for a separable signal (a product of one-dimensional factors) the axis-wise differences would be the natural prior, and the fit is somewhat less accurate there. `:auto` uses, for `:smooth`, 5 for every kernel (higher orders make the smoothing system ill-conditioned, lower orders are less accurate); for `:exact` in 1D the ghost extrapolation's stencil width minus one, at least 5 on uniform grids (so 5 for `:b5`, 7 for the `:b7`-class tables); from 2D one order for all axes, independent of the kernel: 5, the order that completed the gaps best over a range of test functions in two to four dimensions, with 6 a little better in 3D and higher orders showing in the constraint violation. On nonuniform grids the differences are divided differences scaled to plain differences on the local spacing, and `:n3` keeps `q = 4`, the highest order whose completion stays bounded where the data thin out towards the bounds (the `:b` kernels' full-degree ghost extrapolation oscillates there at any `q`, so on such data prefer `:n3`). For data that oscillate everywhere (a chirp) no `q` smooths without biasing the signal, and GCV then leaves `lambda` near zero: the knot count is the regulariser in that case.
  * `lambda::Union{Symbol,Real}=:gcv` (`:smooth` only): the smoothing parameter, or `:gcv` to choose it by generalized cross-validation. The `lambda` returned by a fit reproduces that fit when passed back.
  * `bc::Union{Symbol,Tuple}=:poly` (`:smooth` on uniform grids only): the ghost rule at the ends of the grid, `:poly` (the kernel's full-degree extrapolation, as in `:exact`), `:quadratic` or `:linear`, as a Symbol for every end, a `(left, right)` pair for every axis, or one pair per axis, as in `convolution_interpolation`. A lower degree amplifies the noise less at an end but biases the fit where the signal is steep there; the right choice depends on the data, so `:poly` is the default and a fit that is noisy at a flat end is worth repeating with `:linear` there. Interpolate the fitted grid with the same `bc`. On nonuniform grids the ghosts are the basis's own.
  * `solver::Symbol=:auto` (`:exact` only): how the exact fit is solved. `:auto` uses `:cholesky` in 1D and 2D and `:dual` from 3D, where `:dual` applies. Before it uses `:dual` it checks that the dense system of that solver fits in the machine's memory, and raises an error if it does not. A solver given explicitly is used as given.

      * `:cholesky` factors the Jacobi-equilibrated SPD normal system in the grid unknowns with CHOLMOD. With the narrow kernels its error is set by the fit, not by roundoff. It is the cheapest choice in 1D and 2D; from 3D on the memory and time of the factorization grow steeply with the grid. If the system loses positive definiteness numerically it falls back to `:qr` while that is affordable, and raises an error otherwise.
      * `:qr` solves each multiplier iteration as a sparse least-squares problem via SPQR without forming normal equations; it is several times slower but lowers the roundoff floor of the wide kernels, which rises with the kernel's width. Use `solver=:qr, kernel=:b7` when chasing the deepest accuracy. Its memory grows as the rows times the unknowns of the least-squares system, which limits it to small grids from 3D up.
      * `:dual` finds the grid of `:cholesky` without factorizing in the grid unknowns: it solves a dense system with one unknown per data point and then refines the result by a short iteration on the roughness measure. Its cost follows the point count and not the grid (memory: 8 bytes times the square of the point count), which makes it the faster and lighter choice from 3D and makes exact fits practical in 4D and above. It reproduces the data to rounding. It can be chosen in any dimension, and needs a uniform grid, `Float64` data, and more data points than there are polynomials of total degree below `q` in `D` variables (with `q = 5`: 35 in 3D, 70 in 4D, 126 in 5D). It runs on the available threads.
  * `W::Real=1e6` (`:exact` with `:cholesky` or `:qr`): augmented-Lagrangian penalty weight.
  * `iters::Int=20`, `tol::Real=1e-11` (`:exact` with `:cholesky` or `:qr`): multiplier iteration controls; convergence typically takes 1-2 iterations. `:dual` solves directly and does not iterate.
  * `verbose::Bool=false`: `:exact` prints the constraint violation per iteration, or per solve with `:dual`; `:smooth` prints the grid, `lambda`, cutoff, effective degrees of freedom and estimated noise of the fit.

#### Returns

`(knots, vals, third)`: the tuple of interior knot axes (ranges for a uniform grid, vectors otherwise), the array of fitted interior grid values, and

  * for `:smooth`, `(lambda = λ, noise = σ)`: the smoothing parameter used and the estimated standard deviation of the data about the fit, `√(‖A c − f‖² / (n − edf))` with `edf` the fit's effective degrees of freedom;
  * for `:exact`, `viol`: the final maximum constraint violation.

Construct an interpolant with `convolution_interpolation(knots, vals; kernel, bc=:poly, ...)`, or use `convolution_interpolation(points, values)` which does this directly.

Notes: by default `:exact` solves a sparse SPD system in 1D and 2D (CHOLMOD for `Float64`, dense Cholesky otherwise) and a dense system in the data points from 3D; see `solver`. Exact interpolation requires distinct data points with consistent values. With `:cholesky` and `:qr`, duplicated points with conflicting values are resolved in the least-squares sense and reported through `viol`. `:dual` cannot solve data with duplicated points: it warns, and `viol` shows that the data were not reproduced. `:smooth` always solves in `Float64` (its accuracy is limited by the noise) and casts the fitted grid back to the element type of the data. On nonuniform grids the kernel weights are Float64, as in the nonuniform interpolant itself.




### `convolution_smooth`

```julia
convolution_smooth(knots, values, B)
```

Apply separable Gaussian smoothing to `values` on the uniform grid `knots`. Returns an array of the same size as `values` with noise reduced.

#### Arguments

  * `knots`: grid — an `AbstractVector` (1D) or `NTuple{N,AbstractVector}` (ND). Every axis must be increasing and uniformly spaced.
  * `values`: array of values to smooth, must have `size(values, d) == length(knots[d])`
  * `B`: Gaussian width parameter. Larger `B` means a narrower kernel (less smoothing), smaller `B` means a wider kernel (more smoothing). **B ≤ 0.1 recommended** for effective noise reduction.

An `ArgumentError` is thrown when the knots do not match the data or are not uniform. For noisy data that are scattered or on a nonuniform grid, use the smoothing fit of `convolution_interpolation(points, values)` instead.

#### Returns

Array of smoothed values, same size and element type as `values`.

#### Performance

Smoothing is separable and allocation-free in the inner loop. The Gaussian kernel weights are precomputed once per call — `exp` is evaluated only `2*eqs+1` times regardless of grid size or dimension. The benchmark pages on convinterp.org give timings.

#### Examples

```julia
# 1D smoothing
x = range(0.0, 2π, length=500)
y_noisy = sin.(x) .+ 0.1.*randn(500)
y_smooth = convolution_smooth(x, y_noisy, 0.05)

# 2D smoothing
x = range(0.0, 2π, length=200)
y = range(0.0, 2π, length=200)
z_noisy  = [cos(xi)*sin(yi) for xi in x, yi in y] .+ 0.1.*randn(200,200)
z_smooth = convolution_smooth((x,y), z_noisy, 0.02)
```

See also: [`convolution_gaussian`](@ref), [`convolution_interpolation`](@ref)




### `convolution_gaussian`

```julia
convolution_gaussian(knots, values, B)
convolution_gaussian(knots, values, B; extrap)
```

Construct a Gaussian smoothing interpolant from `values` on the uniform grid `knots`. Unlike `convolution_smooth` which returns an array, this returns an interpolant that can be evaluated at arbitrary locations.

Unlike polynomial convolution kernels which interpolate exactly through data points, the Gaussian kernel smooths: it produces a weighted average of nearby values controlled by `B`. Useful for noisy data where exact interpolation is undesirable.

#### Arguments

  * `knots`: grid — an `AbstractVector` (1D) or `NTuple{N,AbstractVector}` (ND)
  * `values`: array of values, must have `size(values, d) == length(knots[d])`
  * `B`: Gaussian width parameter. Larger `B` means narrower kernel (less smoothing), smaller `B` means wider kernel (more smoothing). `B` up to 0.34 is accepted, above which the kernel is no longer a partition of unity between the knots; `B ≈ 0.1` is the usual choice. `convolution_smooth`, which evaluates on the knots only, takes any `B`.

#### Keyword Arguments

  * `extrap`: extrapolation behavior, default `Throw()`. See [`convolution_interpolation`](@ref).

#### Returns

A `ConvolutionExtrapolation` interpolant supporting evaluation at arbitrary locations.

#### Examples

```julia
x = range(0.0, 2π, length=100)
y_noisy = sin.(x) .+ 0.1.*randn(100)

itp = convolution_gaussian(x, y_noisy, 0.05)
itp(1.5)         # evaluate at arbitrary point
itp.(x)          # evaluate on original grid — smoothed values

# 2D
xs = range(0.0, 2π, length=50)
ys = range(0.0, 2π, length=50)
z_noisy = [sin(x)*cos(y) for x in xs, y in ys] .+ 0.1.*randn(50,50)
itp2 = convolution_gaussian((xs,ys), z_noisy, 0.05)
itp2(1.0, 2.0)   # evaluate at arbitrary 2D point
```

See also: [`convolution_smooth`](@ref), [`convolution_interpolation`](@ref)




### `convolution_resample`

```julia
convolution_resample(knots_in, knots_out, values)
convolution_resample(knots_in, knots_out, values; kernel, derivative, bc)
```

Resample `values` from the uniform grid `knots_in` to the points `knots_out` by high-order convolution interpolation, one axis at a time. For grid-to-grid work this avoids building an interpolant and evaluating it point by point.

#### Arguments

  * `knots_in`: the input grid, an `AbstractVector` in 1D or a tuple with one vector per axis. Every axis must be increasing and uniformly spaced.
  * `knots_out`: the output points of each axis, in the same format. They need not be uniformly spaced, but along every axis they must lie within the range of `knots_in`: resampling does not extrapolate.
  * `values`: the data on `knots_in`, with `size(values, d) == length(knots_in[d])`.

An `ArgumentError` is thrown when the input knots do not match the data, are not uniform, or when an output point lies outside their range. For data on a nonuniform grid, or to extrapolate, build an interpolant with `convolution_interpolation` instead.

#### Keyword Arguments

With keywords, `knots_in` and `knots_out` are tuples in every dimension, so `(x,)` and `(x_new,)` in 1D.

  * `kernel=:b7`: the convolution kernel, a `Symbol` for all axes or a tuple with one per axis, from the kernels of uniform grids (see `convolution_interpolation`).
  * `derivative=0`: the derivative order, an `Int` for all axes or a tuple with one per axis, within the range of the kernel (see `convolution_interpolation`). Antiderivatives are not supported here; use `convolution_interpolation` with a negative `derivative`.
  * `bc=:detect`: the boundary condition, as in `convolution_interpolation` on a uniform grid: `:detect`, `:poly`, `:linear` or `:quadratic`.

#### Axes with few points

The high-order boundary values need a minimum number of points along an axis: with the default `bc = :detect`, 5 for `:a3` to `:a7`, 7 for `:b5` and 9 for `:b7` to `:b13`, and one fewer with `bc = :poly`. An axis with fewer points is resampled without an error, with linear boundary values at its ends: exact for a straight line, less accurate otherwise.

#### Returns

The array of resampled values, with `size(result, d) == length(knots_out[d])`.

#### Examples

```julia
# 1D resampling
x_coarse = range(0.0, 2π, length=20)
x_fine   = range(0.0, 2π, length=200)
y_coarse = sin.(x_coarse)
y_fine   = convolution_resample(x_coarse, x_fine, y_coarse)

# 1D with a keyword: the knots as one-element tuples
y_fine_b5 = convolution_resample((x_coarse,), (x_fine,), y_coarse; kernel=:b5)

# 2D resampling
xs = range(0.0, 2π, length=20)
ys = range(0.0, 2π, length=20)
z  = [sin(x)*cos(y) for x in xs, y in ys]
xs_fine = range(0.0, 2π, length=100)
ys_fine = range(0.0, 2π, length=100)
z_fine  = convolution_resample((xs, ys), (xs_fine, ys_fine), z)

# Resample and differentiate in one pass
z_dx = convolution_resample((xs, ys), (xs_fine, ys_fine), z; derivative=(1, 0))
```

See also: [`convolution_interpolation`](@ref), [`convolution_smooth`](@ref)




### `convolution_suggest`

```julia
convolution_suggest(itp; tol = 1e-6, samples = 8)
```

Where a one-dimensional interpolant on a nonuniform grid needs knots to be accurate: the midpoints of the intervals in which its estimated error exceeds `tol`.

A `b` kernel of degree `p` reproduces polynomials up to that degree on a nonuniform grid, so the leading part of its error comes from the term of degree `p + 1` in the data. The estimate is the product of two factors. The first is the size of that term: the divided difference of order `p + 1` of the data over the `p + 2` knots nearest the interval, taken as the largest of the interval and its two neighbours. The second is the error the kernel itself makes on the monomial of degree `p + 1` on these knots, measured by interpolating it. This is the test that `bc = :detect` applies at the boundary of a uniform grid, carried to every interval and scaled to an error in the units of the data.

The estimate is also large where a wide kernel oscillates on a grid that is too coarse for it, most often near the ends of the grid, so the same knots cure that.

Evaluate the data at the returned points and pass both to [`convolution_refine`](@ref). Repeat until nothing is returned, with a limit on the number of passes: where the data have a kink or a jump the estimate does not fall and the interval is returned every time.

The estimate uses only the knots and their values. A feature of the data that lies entirely between two knots cannot be seen, and at rounding level the differences are noise, so a tolerance near the precision of the data flags intervals without end.

#### Keyword Arguments

  * `tol::Real=1e-6`: the estimated error that calls for a knot, as a fraction of the range of all the data.
  * `samples::Int=8`: the number of points inside each interval at which the error on the monomial is measured.

```julia
# the data
f(x) = 1 / (1 + 25x^2)
# nonuniform knots
x = [-1.0, -0.8, -0.55, -0.3, -0.1, 0.0, 0.15, 0.3, 0.5, 0.75, 0.9, 1.0]
# a coarse interpolant
itp = convolution_interpolation(x, f.(x); kernel = :b5)
# refine, with a limit on the passes
for pass in 1:20
    # midpoints of the intervals that need a knot
    x_new = convolution_suggest(itp; tol = 1e-6)
    # the estimate is below tol everywhere
    isempty(x_new) && break
    # the interpolant with knots added there
    itp = convolution_refine(itp, x_new, f.(x_new))
end
```

See also: [`convolution_refine`](@ref).




### `convolution_refine`

```julia
convolution_refine(itp, x_new, values_new)
```

Add knots to a one-dimensional interpolant on a nonuniform grid and return the new interpolant.

`x_new` holds the positions of the new knots and `values_new` the data values there (two numbers for a single knot). The result is the interpolant that `convolution_interpolation` builds on the merged knots and values, with the same kernel, derivative order and extrapolation, but only the weights near the new knots are computed: with a `:b` kernel an interval keeps its weights unless one of the knots it is built from is new. Those are the M knots on either side of it, with M = 5 for `:b5` up to 9 for `:b13`, so one new knot costs 2M intervals however many knots the grid has. The other kernels of nonuniform grids (`:n3`, `:a0`, `:a1`) have closed-form weights and are simply rebuilt.

New knots may lie anywhere, also outside the old grid, but not on an existing knot. The interpolant passed in is left unchanged.

Use [`convolution_suggest`](@ref) to find where an interpolant needs knots.

```julia
# nonuniform knots
x = [0.0, 0.1, 0.25, 0.3, 0.5, 0.55, 0.7, 0.9, 1.0]
# interpolant on them
itp = convolution_interpolation(x, sin.(x); kernel = :b5)
# where knots are to be added
x_new = [0.4, 0.8]
# the interpolant on all eleven knots
itp2 = convolution_refine(itp, x_new, sin.(x_new))
```

See also: [`convolution_interpolation`](@ref), [`convolution_suggest`](@ref).




## Types

### `ConvolutionInterpolation`

```julia
ConvolutionInterpolation{T,N,NI,TCoefs<:AbstractArray{T,N},
                             Axs<:Tuple,KA,DT,K,EQ,KBC,DOT,LZ,DI,SZ,NU}
```

Convolution interpolation on uniform and nonuniform grids. On uniform axes the kernel weights are computed exactly from each kernel's polynomial pieces (see `_column_rows`), so evaluation is exact to rounding for every kernel, derivative and integral order, and independent of the grid size. On nonuniform axes the cell is found by a binary search in the knots; the weights of the `b` kernels come from per-interval polynomial tables computed at construction (see `precompute_nonuniform_b_all`), and the closed-form kernels (`:n3`, `:a0`, `:a1`) adapt their weights to the local spacing at evaluation.

#### Type Parameters

  * `T`: Element type of the interpolated values
  * `N`: Number of dimensions
  * `NI`: Number of integral dimensions (derivative order -1)
  * `TCoefs`: Type of the coefficient array
  * `Axs`: Type of the knots (typically a tuple of ranges)
  * `KA`: Kernel type per dimension (`nothing` for polynomial kernels)
  * `DT`: Dimension type for dispatch (`Val{N}` for N ≤ 3, `HigherDimension{N}` otherwise)
  * `K`: Kernel symbol type for dispatch (e.g. `HigherOrderKernel{(:b5, :b5)}`)
  * `EQ`: Kernel stencil half-widths per dimension
  * `KBC`: Boundary condition type
  * `DOT`: Derivative order type
  * `LZ`: Lazy mode flag (`Val{true}` or `Val{false}`)
  * `DI`: Integral dimension type for dispatch
  * `SZ`: Type of the data domain size
  * `NU`: Type of the per-axis nonuniform data (a tuple of `Nothing` on a uniform grid)

#### Fields

  * `coefs::TCoefs`: Coefficients, extended with ghost points (eager mode) or raw values (lazy mode)
  * `domain_size::SZ`: Size of the original data array
  * `knots::Axs`: Knots of each dimension, extended with ghost knots in eager mode
  * `h::NTuple{N,T}`: Grid spacing per dimension (one on nonuniform dimensions)
  * `x0::NTuple{N,T}`: First (extended) knot per dimension
  * `kernel::KA`: Kernel type per dimension
  * `dimension::DT`: Dimension type for dispatch
  * `kernel_sym::K`: Kernel symbols for dispatch
  * `eqs::EQ`: Kernel stencil half-widths per dimension
  * `bc::KBC`: Boundary conditions per dimension
  * `derivative_order::DOT`: Derivative orders per dimension
  * `lazy::LZ`: If `Val(true)`, ghost points are computed on the fly near the boundaries
  * `anchor::NTuple{N,T}`: Point where antiderivatives are zero, per integral dimension
  * `dim_integral::DI`: Integral dimension type for dispatch
  * `integral_taylor::NTuple{N,Matrix{T}}`: For each integral dimension of order m, the exact values K*{m-r}(eqs - j) of the coefficients near the anchor (see `*anchor*taylor*table`)
  * `integral_entries::NTuple{N,Matrix{T}}`: For each integral dimension, the exact polynomials (in the position within the cell) that near-anchor coefficients contribute left of the stencil
  * `integral_tails::Vector{Vector{Array{T,N}}}`: For at most 3 integral dimensions, the left tails of every region: entry `mask` holds one array per combination of powers of the positions within the cell (see `_build_region_tails`)
  * `nonuniform::NU`: Per axis, `nothing` on a uniform axis; on a nonuniform axis the per-interval weight tables of a `b` kernel (`Vector{Matrix{T}}`), or `Val(:nonuniform)` for a kernel whose weights are computed from the local spacing at evaluation (`:n3`, `:a0`, `:a1`)




### `ConvolutionExtrapolation`

```julia
ConvolutionExtrapolation{T,N,ITPT<:ConvolutionInterpolation,ET<:AbstractExtrapolation}
```

A structure that combines a convolution interpolation with boundary condition extrapolation techniques.

#### Type Parameters

  * `T`: The data type of the interpolated values
  * `N`: The dimensionality of the data (number of dimensions)
  * `ITPT`: The specific type of convolution interpolation being used
  * `ET`: The boundary condition extrapolation technique

#### Fields

  * `itp::ITPT`: The underlying interpolation object
  * `et::ET`: The extrapolation technique (boundary condition)

#### Details

This structure extends the functionality of convolution interpolation objects by defining  behavior for points outside the domain of the original data through various extrapolation  techniques.

When called as a function, the object automatically determines whether the requested point is within the interpolation domain. If so, it uses direct interpolation; if not, it applies the specified boundary condition to handle the extrapolation.

This struct is not simple to use manually, so it is recommended to use the `convolution_interpolation` function.
